questions.stem: The specific latent heat of fusion of a substance is the quantity of heat required to

options.text: raise the temperature of 1 kg of the substance by 1 K
change 1 kg of the solid to liquid at its melting point without change of temperature
change 1 kg of the liquid to vapour at its boiling point
raise the temperature of the whole solid to its melting point

questions.explanation: Fusion means melting, and latent heat is the energy supplied while the temperature stays constant. The definition therefore refers to exactly 1 kg changing from solid to liquid at the melting point with no temperature change.

distractorRationale.a: That is the definition of specific heat capacity, where the temperature does change
distractorRationale.c: That is the specific latent heat of vaporisation, a different quantity with a much larger value
distractorRationale.d: Warming a solid up to its melting point involves mcΔθ, not latent heat

questions.stem: The SI unit of specific latent heat is

options.text: $\text{J}\,\text{kg}^{-1}$
$\text{J}\,\text{K}^{-1}$
$\text{J}$

questions.explanation: From $Q = ml$, we get $l = \frac{Q}{m}$, so the unit is joule per kilogram. No kelvin appears because a change of state happens at constant temperature — this is a quick way to tell latent heat and specific heat capacity apart.

distractorRationale.b: This is specific heat capacity, which includes a temperature term
distractorRationale.c: This is heat capacity of a whole body
distractorRationale.d: The joule alone is the unit of the heat Q, not of the specific latent heat

questions.stem: The temperature of a pure substance remains constant while it is melting because the heat supplied is used to

options.text: increase the average kinetic energy of the molecules
overcome the forces of attraction between the molecules
expand the container holding the substance
destroy some of the molecules

questions.explanation: Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the molecules. During melting the supplied energy does work against the intermolecular forces, increasing the potential energy of the molecules while their average kinetic energy is unchanged, so the thermometer reading stays fixed.

distractorRationale.a: If the average kinetic energy rose, the temperature would rise too, which is not what is observed
distractorRationale.c: Any expansion of the container absorbs a negligible amount of energy and would not hold the temperature constant
distractorRationale.d: Molecules are not destroyed in a physical change of state; the substance is chemically unchanged

questions.stem: Calculate the heat required to melt 0.50 kg of ice at 0 °C into water at 0 °C. Take the specific latent heat of fusion of ice as 3.36 × 10⁵ J/kg. Give your answer in joules.
questions.explanation: $Q = ml_f = 0.50 \times 3.36 \times 10^5 = 1.68 \times 10^5 = 168\,000\ \text{J}$. There is no temperature term because both the ice and the resulting water are at 0 °C.

questions.stem: Calculate the heat required to change 0.20 kg of water at 100 °C completely into steam at 100 °C. Take the specific latent heat of vaporisation of water as 2.26 × 10⁶ J/kg. Give your answer in joules.
questions.explanation: $Q = ml_v = 0.20 \times 2.26 \times 10^6 = 4.52 \times 10^5 = 452\,000\ \text{J}$. Compare this with the 84 000 J needed merely to raise the same water from 0 °C to 100 °C — boiling it away costs more than five times as much.

questions.stem: The specific latent heat of vaporisation of water is much larger than its specific latent heat of fusion because during vaporisation

options.text: the temperature of the water rises considerably
the molecules must be completely separated and work is done against atmospheric pressure
water molecules are chemically broken into hydrogen and oxygen
the mass of the water increases

questions.explanation: In melting, molecules only need enough energy to slide past one another and stay in contact. In vaporisation they must be pulled fully apart against the intermolecular attraction, and the vapour must also push back the atmosphere as it expands. Both effects demand far more energy per kilogram.

distractorRationale.a: The temperature stays constant at 100 °C throughout boiling — that is the defining feature of latent heat
distractorRationale.c: Boiling is a physical change; the molecules remain H₂O
distractorRationale.d: Mass is conserved during a change of state

questions.stem: Calculate the total heat required to convert 2.0 kg of ice at 0 °C into water at 100 °C. Take the specific latent heat of fusion of ice as 3.36 × 10⁵ J/kg and the specific heat capacity of water as 4200 J/kg/K. Give your answer in joules.
questions.explanation: Stage 1, melting the ice: $Q_1 = ml_f = 2.0 \times 3.36 \times 10^5 = 672\,000\ \text{J}$. Stage 2, heating the water from 0 °C to 100 °C: $Q_2 = mc\Delta\theta = 2.0 \times 4200 \times 100 = 840\,000\ \text{J}$. Total $= 672\,000 + 840\,000 = 1\,512\,000\ \text{J}$.

questions.stem: On a graph of temperature against time for a substance being heated steadily, a horizontal (flat) portion of the graph indicates that

options.text: the heater has been switched off
a change of state is taking place
the substance has stopped absorbing heat
the specific heat capacity has become zero

questions.explanation: The heater keeps supplying energy at the same rate, but during a change of state that energy goes into separating molecules rather than raising their kinetic energy. The temperature therefore stays constant, producing a flat section, and both states coexist for as long as it lasts.

distractorRationale.a: The question specifies steady heating throughout, so the supply has not stopped
distractorRationale.c: The substance is still absorbing heat — as latent heat rather than as a temperature rise
distractorRationale.d: Specific heat capacity is a fixed property of the material; it does not vanish

questions.stem: What mass of ice at 0 °C must be added to 1.0 kg of water at 40 °C so that the final mixture is water at 0 °C? Take l_f = 3.36 × 10⁵ J/kg and c_water = 4200 J/kg/K. Give your answer in kilograms.
questions.explanation: Heat released by the water cooling from 40 °C to 0 °C is $mc\Delta\theta = 1.0 \times 4200 \times 40 = 168\,000\ \text{J}$. All of it goes into melting ice, so $m = \frac{Q}{l_f} = \frac{168\,000}{3.36 \times 10^5} = 0.50\ \text{kg}$. Note the melted ice needs no further heating because the final temperature is 0 °C.

questions.stem: An immersion heater rated 840 W is placed in a funnel of ice at 0 °C for 5.0 minutes. Assuming all the energy goes into melting the ice and taking l_f = 3.36 × 10⁵ J/kg, calculate the mass of ice melted. Give your answer in kilograms.
questions.explanation: Energy supplied $= Pt = 840 \times (5.0 \times 60) = 252\,000\ \text{J}$. Mass melted $= \frac{Q}{l_f} = \frac{252\,000}{3.36 \times 10^5} = 0.75\ \text{kg}$. Remember to convert the 5.0 minutes into 300 s before multiplying by the power.

questions.stem: The process of melting involves a change of state from solid to liquid. During this process, the temperature of the substance remains constant because:

options.text: the heat energy is used to increase the kinetic energy of the molecules.
the heat energy is absorbed to break the bonds between molecules.
the heat energy is lost to the surroundings.
the pressure remains constant.

questions.explanation: During the melting process, heat energy is absorbed by the substance to break the intermolecular bonds that hold the solid structure together. This energy does not increase the temperature but rather facilitates the change of state from solid to liquid.

distractorRationale.a: This option incorrectly suggests that the energy increases molecular motion, which is not the case during melting.
distractorRationale.c: This option is incorrect because heat is absorbed, not lost, during melting.
distractorRationale.d: While pressure may remain constant, it does not explain why temperature does not change during melting.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best describes specific latent heat?

options.text: It is the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C.
It is the amount of heat required to change the state of 1 kg of a substance without changing its temperature.
It is the amount of heat released when 1 kg of a substance freezes.
It is the total heat energy contained in 1 kg of a substance.

questions.explanation: Specific latent heat is defined as the amount of heat required to change the state of 1 kg of a substance without a change in temperature. This definition applies to both fusion and vaporization processes.

distractorRationale.a: This option describes specific heat capacity, not latent heat.
distractorRationale.c: This option only refers to the freezing process, not the general definition of latent heat.
distractorRationale.d: This option is misleading as it does not specifically define latent heat.

questions.stem: What happens to the temperature of a substance during boiling?

options.text: It increases steadily.
It decreases steadily.
It remains constant until all the liquid has turned to gas.
It fluctuates randomly.

questions.explanation: During boiling, the temperature of the liquid remains constant at its boiling point until all of the liquid has been converted to gas. This is because the heat energy added is used for the phase change rather than increasing the temperature.

distractorRationale.a: This option is incorrect as the temperature does not increase during boiling.
distractorRationale.b: This option incorrectly suggests a decrease in temperature during boiling.
distractorRationale.d: Temperature does not fluctuate randomly during boiling.

questions.stem: The formula Q = ml is used to calculate:

options.text: the heat required to change the temperature of a substance.
the heat required for a change of state.
the total energy of a substance.
the work done by a substance.

questions.explanation: The equation Q = ml relates the heat energy (Q) to the mass (m) of a substance and the specific latent heat (l) during a change of state, either during melting or vaporization.

distractorRationale.a: This option describes the heat transfer related to temperature changes, not a change of state.
distractorRationale.c: This option is incorrect as Q = ml specifically refers to latent heat calculations.
distractorRationale.d: This option does not relate to the heat energy during a change of state.

questions.explanation: To calculate the heat absorbed, use the formula Q = ml. Here, m = 0.5 kg and l = 334,000 J/kg, so Q = 0.5 * 334,000 = 167,000 J.

distractorRationale.a: This option is incorrect; it miscalculates the heat absorbed.
distractorRationale.c: This option does not apply to the mass and specific latent heat given.
distractorRationale.d: This option is incorrect as it significantly overestimates the required heat.

questions.stem: Why is the specific latent heat of vaporization generally higher than that of fusion?

options.text: More energy is required to break the bonds of a liquid.
The temperature of the liquid is higher.
Vaporization involves breaking all intermolecular forces.
Fusion occurs at a lower temperature.

questions.explanation: The specific latent heat of vaporization is higher than that of fusion because vaporization requires the complete breaking of intermolecular forces to convert a liquid into a gas, whereas fusion only requires breaking some bonds to convert a solid into a liquid.

distractorRationale.a: This option is misleading as it does not fully explain the reason for the difference in latent heats.
distractorRationale.b: The temperature alone does not explain the energy required for phase changes.
distractorRationale.d: While fusion occurs at lower temperatures, this does not explain the difference in latent heat values.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true regarding latent heat during a phase change?

Latent heat is absorbed when a substance vaporizes.

questions.explanation: Latent heat is absorbed during vaporization as the substance transitions from liquid to gas, while it is released during condensation. It is important to note that latent heat values vary among different substances.

questions.stem: During the melting process, the heat energy supplied is used to break the bonds between particles rather than increasing the temperature. This results in a constant temperature. Which of the following best explains this phenomenon?
